As far as I can tell, you seem to be running into floating-point precision problems due to the small (per tick) rotation values.

The conversion of the target rotation into a quaternion (as needed by Jolt) results in a value of `(0, 0.0001454441, 0, 1)`. This should rightfully be more like `(0, 0.0001454441, 0, 0.9999999894)`, but ends up rounding here during normalization, due to the inherent lack of precision with 32-bit floats:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/78c6632eb174aabb2790975cf83e28fee065b43d/modules/jolt_physics/objects/jolt_body_3d.cpp#L212

... which then leads to the calculated delta rotation being treated as zero here:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/78c6632eb174aabb2790975cf83e28fee065b43d/thirdparty/jolt_physics/Jolt/Math/Quat.inl#L142-L146

... as part of this:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/78c6632eb174aabb2790975cf83e28fee065b43d/thirdparty/jolt_physics/Jolt/Physics/Body/MotionProperties.inl#L19-L23

Unfortunately building Godot with `precision=double` won't help you either, since Jolt limits its use of double-precision to things like absolute positions.

I'm seeing that there might be alternative ways to implement the extraction of angles from a quaternion that avoids relying on the `w` component altogether, but I don't know enough about quaternions to say whether that's a good idea or not.

Any thoughts on this, @jrouwe?

I'll make a fix to the angular velocity calculation for very small angles. The reason why there is translation (case 2) is that Jolt calculates the center of mass (COM) differently than Godot Physics: (note I didn't verify the COM for godot physics, but as far as I know it doesn't attempt to calculate it but just takes the transform of the rigid body) In any case, when an object is rotating around another point than it's COM, you have to set a linear and angular velocity. This makes an assumption that the equation to achieve that rotation is linear, which it isn't so you get some drift. The drift is bigger the further the rotation point is from the COM. The simple fix for this is to set the COM so that the object rotates around it and no linear velocity is needed: I guess this could be done by default when a body is kinematic. But I assume you can switch between dynamic and kinematic at runtime. This would add some extra complexity of updating the COM. I'm not sure if it's worth it to fix that. B.t.w. instead of doing `rotate_y` every frame, I would just set a constant angular velocity once.

> note I didn't verify the COM for godot physics, but as far as I know it doesn't attempt to calculate it but just takes the transform of the rigid body

It uses the shape's local transform as its center-of-mass, along with a "bad AABB approximation" for its principal moments of inertia:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/233a5aeb4d23b569bb0c711825bb31978313d4ca/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_body_3d.cpp#L84-L85

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/233a5aeb4d23b569bb0c711825bb31978313d4ca/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_shape_3d.cpp#L1071-L1079

... but it seems center-of-mass is not taken into account with kinematic bodies in general (see below).

> I guess this could be done by default when a body is kinematic. But I assume you can switch between dynamic and kinematic at runtime. This would add some extra complexity of updating the COM. I'm not sure if it's worth it to fix that.

You can switch between them at runtime, yes, using the `freeze` and `freeze_mode` properties found on `RigidBody3D`.

> B.t.w. instead of doing `rotate_y` every frame, I would just set a constant angular velocity once.

The linear/angular velocity properties are (confusingly) used for surface velocities when a `RigidBody3D` is in either `FREEZE_MODE_KINEMATIC` or `FREEZE_MODE_STATIC`. There is no way to move a kinematic body by setting the velocities, like in Jolt.

---

It does look like there might be a significant discrepancy with regards to kinematic bodies that I hadn't picked up on before, which is that Godot Physics simply doesn't take center-of-mass into account at all when transforming a kinematic body:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/233a5aeb4d23b569bb0c711825bb31978313d4ca/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_body_3d.cpp#L615-L629

(`get_transform()` is the start, `new_transform` is the target, center-of-mass is stored separately as `center_of_mass`.)

I'm tempted to say that Godot Physics is wrong here, but if a kinematic body essentially has infinite mass, can it even be considered to have a center-of-mass? So maybe it should just behave like any other non-physics node as far as transformations go? I wonder what other physics engines do in this case.

> The linear/angular velocity properties are (confusingly) used for surface velocities when a RigidBody3D is in either FREEZE_MODE_KINEMATIC or FREEZE_MODE_STATIC. There is no way to move a kinematic body by setting the velocities, like in Jolt.

Ok, that is really really weird. The whole point of a kinematic body is that it is moved by setting a velocity.

> I'm tempted to say that Godot Physics is wrong here, but if a kinematic body essentially has infinite mass, can it even be considered to have a center-of-mass? So maybe it should just behave like any other non-physics node as far as transformations go? I wonder what other physics engines do in this case.

I think the point of rotation is basically a choice you can freely make for kinematic bodies. I haven't tested this, but I wouldn't be surprised if other physics engines also rotate around the body transform instead of the COM in that case. Because it simplifies the math a bit I made a choice really early on in the development of Jolt to always reason from the COM (a decision that is not easy to change at this point).

> Ok, that is really really weird. The whole point of a kinematic body is that it is moved by setting a velocity.

Godot Physics seems to treat the velocities of kinematic bodies more as a byproduct of the transformation, rather than the other way around, as they don't take part in any velocity integration, which seems a little bit backwards:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/ebbdef7830e9dd0a2c293ef2f951a7a2d3ada14e/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_body_3d.cpp#L701-L709

I guess that might explain why Godot Physics doesn't suffer from as much precision loss here, since there's no round-tripping of transform-to-velocity-to-transform.

> I think the point of rotation is basically a choice you can freely make for kinematic bodies.

I'll see if I can find some time to test a few other engines, to see how they deal with this. However, seeing as how you can still just force a custom COM of `(0, 0, 0)` to get the Godot-like behavior with Jolt, it does seem a tad more flexible to leave things as-is and just documenting it instead.

Thanks for investigating this @mihe and @jrouwe . I agree it should be mentioned in docs, I didn't even think to take center of mass into the account when moving kinematic body as it's a physics property and it's specifically mentioned in the docs that kinematic is moved through code and ignores any forces.

Let me investigate this a bit more. Maybe I can find a way to make this work.

In any case, the fix for point 1 has been merged now, so if you build from source then the small angle rotation should be fixed.

I started investigating this with the latest version on 'master' and I cannot reproduce the bug anymore. Without the COM override, at 10 deg/s, it seems to behave fine now. I tried speeds from 0.1 - 1000 deg/s, they all seem fine. I even tried forcing the COM to (10000, 0, 0) and it still rotates exactly around the visual center. It appears that the fix to the small angle rotations fixed this issue completely. @patrykkalinowski Can you please confirm?
I've locally backed out #115327 and then I can reproduce the issue again at 10 deg/s, so I'm pretty sure this was the fix.
@jrouwe Tested minimal reproduction project on 4.7dev1, looks fixed. Thank you!
